stories.headline: ‘We Have to Take Over’: Far-Right Extremists Want to Seize Control of the GOP
stories.claim: Far-right groups and figures say the midterm results give them an opening to take over the Republican Party.
stories.summary: WIRED reports that white nationalist Nick Fuentes and other far-right groups, including Christian nationalists and the Proud Boys, see the US midterm results as an opportunity to take control of the Republican Party. Fuentes urged supporters to vote Democrat on Election Day and then claimed credit for the Democratic sweep, calling it the 'Groyper Effect'. The Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights found that 338 of 476 called races involving far-right-linked statewide candidates were won, a 71 percent win rate. Several states passed ballot measures on trans athletes, voter ID and immigration. Some activists are planning events around the 3 January certification of the results in Congress, though experts have not yet seen explicit calls for violence.
key_points: Nick Fuentes urged followers to vote Democrat on Election Day, then claimed credit for the Democratic victory.
Far-right groups say the GOP must be taken over from within, with calls for a 'hostile takeover' at state level.
IREHR tracked 535 far-right-linked candidates; 338 of 476 called statewide races were won, a 71 percent win rate.
Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington approved bans on trans athletes in female sports, among other ballot measures.
Jake Lang plans an event in DC on 3 January, the day Congress certifies the midterm results.
Experts say they have not yet seen explicit calls for violence from the groups they track.

stories.headline: Stocks rally as investors snap up tech shares at lower prices
stories.claim: European and Asian shares rise on AI chip buying and falling oil, as Brent drops toward $90 on Iran war peace hopes.
stories.summary: European stocks rose on Tuesday 10 November, extending Monday's gains, with the FTSE 100 up 0.73%, the CAC 40 up 1.20% and the DAX up 1.14% in early trading. Asian markets rallied strongly, with South Korea's Kospi up 4.5%, Taiwan's Taiex up 2.5% and Japan's Nikkei 225 up 2.9%, led by AI-linked chipmakers. TSMC reported October revenue up 59.7% year on year, and SoftBank shares jumped 13.9% before its earnings. Brent fell to around $90 a barrel, down about 20% this month, as traders bet on an end to the Iran war after Donald Trump said there was positive momentum towards ending it. China's October exports rose 35.2% and imports 41.6%, putting it on course for a record annual trade surplus above $1 trillion for the first ten months. Analysts warned that investors remain selective about returns on AI spending.

Kospi surged 4.5%, Taiex rose 2.5% and Nikkei 225 closed 2.9% higher, helped by SK hynix, Samsung, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron.

Brent crude fell towards $90 a barrel and WTI to about $84.70, both down roughly 20% this month on hopes of ending the Iran war.
Nvidia shares rose about 1% premarket after reports that the FBI was looking into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy.
China's exports rose 35.2% in October and imports 41.6%; the US dollar traded at 157.91 yen and the euro at $1.1249.

stories.headline: Trump taps Palantir security chief to run battered US cyber defense agency
stories.claim: Trump has nominated Palantir's chief information security officer, Michael LoSapio, to lead the US cyber agency CISA.
stories.summary: President Donald Trump has nominated Michael LoSapio, Palantir's chief information security officer, to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the US civilian cyber defence agency. The nomination was announced on Monday 9 November and would end a nearly two-year vacancy since Jen Easterly left in January 2025. CISA has reportedly lost more than 1,000 staff, about a third of its workforce, since Trump returned to office, and acting director Nick Andersen has run the agency since February. LoSapio would be Trump's second pick after Sean Plankey withdrew in April. Confirmation hearings are likely to focus on Palantir's government work, including its contracts with immigration authorities and controversies in the UK over NHS data.

stories.headline: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law

The five judges ruled that two sections of the Sexual Offences Act 1986, which criminalise buggery and serious indecency between men, violate his fundamental rights to private and family life under the 1976 constitution. The laws carry prison terms of up to five years and have not been enforced recently, but campaigners say they send an intimidating message. stories.headline: Study: Data center energy costs hit lower income households hardest

In an interview with The Register at a Las Vegas event, AMD's Madhu Rangarajan described Verano plus AMD GPUs as the rival to Nvidia's Vera Rubin integrated CPU-GPU platform. CPU-to-GPU links use xGMI at up to 112 Gbps per lane, which AMD says is close to PCIe 7.0 bandwidth levels.

stories.claim: Nvidia unveils GR00T 2, a robot foundation model that learns tasks from human videos with reduced teleoperation.
stories.summary: Nvidia has published research on GR00T 2, a new AI foundation model for robots designed to reduce the need for slow, expensive teleoperation. Instead of mapping camera images and language straight to motor commands, it predicts the next movement and a short video of what comes next, letting it transfer human movements from video to robot arms. It was trained on a cluster of more than 1,000 GB300 chips and about 400,000 hours of head-camera footage of people. In lab tests, success rates ranged from 10% to 80% depending on the task. stories.headline: Congress’s Permitting Bill Is a ‘Massive Giveaway’ to the AI Data Center Industry, Critics Warn
stories.claim: US Senate advanced a bipartisan energy permitting bill (BAAJA) that critics say would boost AI data centres and gas power.
stories.summary: The US Senate voted on Monday to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a permitting bill meant to speed up new energy infrastructure. Supporters, including labour leaders and clean energy advocates, say it will create jobs, unlock wind and solar, and modernise the grid, and its sponsors want it passed before Congress ends in January. Critics, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, argue it would accelerate AI data centre construction, speed up gas projects, weaken environmental and tribal protections, and expand data centres on federal land. The bill also requires data centres to pay the full cost of the grid upgrades they trigger, with one study estimating about $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years. President Trump urged its passage, making it a first major test for Democrats after the midterms.
key_points: The Senate voted on Monday to advance BAAJA, a bipartisan energy permitting bill, with sponsors aiming for passage before January.
Supporters say the bill will create jobs, speed up wind and solar, and modernise transmission lines.
Critics say it would fast-track gas-powered data centres and weaken environmental and tribal protections.
The bill would require data centres to pay for the grid upgrades they trigger; one study estimates $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years, about $35 billion more than current policy.
Data centres on federal land are a particular concern, with at least 17 active applications reported in several western states.
President Trump urged the Senate to pass the bill, while hundreds of groups have written to Congress urging changes.

stories.headline: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
stories.claim: Analysis argues the US data-centre backlash is driven mainly by electricity supply and grid strain, not just culture-war politics.
stories.summary: Writing from Ashburn in Virginia's Data Center Alley, the MIT Technology Review argues the public backlash against data centres is largely about electricity rather than a culture war. Loudoun County data centres mostly connect to the grid, with Dominion Energy supplying power largely from natural gas. Newer rural AI campuses often bring their own gas turbines or diesel generators because local grids cannot supply them. New Virginia rules require data centres to pay the full cost of new transmission lines, and developers expect possible curbs during peak demand. The author argues the industry's power needs, not public opposition, are the main constraint on expansion.
key_points: The average Loudoun County data centre has about 54 megawatts of capacity, and most connect to Dominion Energy's grid.
Virginia has introduced rules requiring data centres to pay fully for new transmission lines.
Developers expect new rules that could cut them off from grid power during peak demand.
Large AI campuses often use on-site gas turbines, which release air pollutants.
Anthropic has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines, according to the article.

stories.market_take: Power and gas-turbine suppliers could benefit from the shift to on-site generation.

stories.headline: Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions
stories.claim: Researchers propose counterfactual world models that let robots predict what would have happened under other actions.
stories.summary: Researchers including Randall Balestriero, Kerda Varaku and Yann LeCun have published a pre-print paper proposing counterfactual world models, which let robots reason about actions they did not take. The method uses the gap between prediction and observed outcome to infer hidden factors, such as a current affecting a boat, and then predicts alternative actions. In simulated tasks, a robot using the approach reached its goal in 35 to 69 percent of events, against 14 to 23 percent for a planner ignoring the observed outcome. The approach uses off-the-shelf encoders with a small trained predictor. The work is a pre-print and has not been peer reviewed.
key_points: The pre-print paper is titled 'Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus'.
The method uses the difference between predicted and actual outcomes to infer hidden disturbances.
In simulated tasks, success rose to 35 to 69 percent, against 14 to 23 percent for a baseline planner.
With two more attempts on the same event, success rose to 51 to 97 percent in the authors' tests.
The approach uses existing encoders such as DINOv2 and MAE with only a small predictor trained on top.
The authors claim the method is provably limited in error, but the work is at pre-print stage and not peer reviewed.

stories.summary: Former Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina has requested a new passport and identity card, according to a letter seen by Reuters. The request is the clearest sign yet that she is preparing to act on her plan to return from self-imposed exile in India in December. stories.headline: British troops being sent abroad to disrupt cyber attacks
stories.claim: The British Army's cyber force has deployed 'hunt force' troops abroad to disrupt cyber attacks before they spread, the commander says.
stories.summary: Major General Mike Fayers, commander of the Defence Cyber and Electromagnetic Force, told The Times that British soldiers are being sent abroad to hunt hackers in countries that agree to the deployment. The unit, called a hunt force, was unveiled in last year's strategic defence review, and its existence had not been made public before. The move follows widespread cyber disruption across Europe, including an attack on France's national blood bank and fridge sabotage at shops. Fayers said he hopes the force will grow over the next few years. The Ministry of Defence reported 90,000 attacks from state-linked sources over two years, and the government's plan to reach 3% of GDP on defence is due at next year's spending review.

stories.headline: Trump is ending military aid to Israel – what difference will it make?
stories.claim: Trump says US will end its military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, a shift from a 10-year aid pact.
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump announced that Washington will end military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, ahead of the US midterm elections. The decision cuts a 10-year memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8bn a year, made up of $3.3bn in foreign military financing and $500m for missile defence. The Independent reports that Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had long wanted to wean Israel off US support, and that Trump said Netanyahu first proposed the idea months ago. Experts say the economic impact on Israel could be significant, as Israel must fund purchases of US weapons itself, while joint missile defence cooperation may continue under some carve-out. The Wall Street Journal estimates Israel faces about $10bn in outstanding orders that must now be paid for.

The UK and European states have reportedly imposed some targeted sanctions on Israel, adding economic pressure.
stories.market_take: Mainly a defence-sector and Israeli fiscal story; US defence contractors selling to Israel could see some pressure on orders, though the impact looks modest.

stories.headline: Turkiye pushes electrification top of climate agenda as COP31 set to open
stories.claim: Turkiye launches a non-binding 35-by-35 electrification pledge as COP31 opens in Antalya.
stories.summary: The UN climate conference COP31 opens in Antalya, Turkiye, on Monday with electrification as a central theme. Turkiye is launching the non-binding 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which aims for electricity to make up at least 35% of global energy demand by 2035. Electricity currently accounts for about one-fifth of global final energy consumption, according to the IEA. Climate advocates say the pledge does not require the extra electricity to come from low-carbon sources, sparking debate over whether it counts as climate progress. The conference takes place against the backdrop of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted Strait of Hormuz oil shipments and pushed Asian nations towards more coal.

stories.headline: China extends suspensions of 24% tariff on US goods, port fees on US ships for two months
stories.claim: China extends suspension of 24% tariff on US goods and special port fees on US-linked ships for two months.
stories.summary: China has extended the suspension of its additional 24% tariff on US imports for two months, starting from 10 November, while keeping a 10% tariff in place. It also extended the suspension of special port fees on US-linked ships until 10 January 2027, and continues to pause a probe into shipping and shipbuilding supply chain security. The move follows the September Washington summit between the Chinese and US leaders, where both sides proposed reciprocal tariff cuts worth about US$60 billion, though the plan is not yet finalised. China says it is responding to US plans to use Section 301 tariffs to replace tariffs struck down by courts under IEEPA, and it will adjust countermeasures as needed.

stories.summary: The Philippine economy grew 2.1% in July to September, down from an upwardly revised 2.4% in the previous quarter and near its weakest pace in more than five years, according to official data reported by Reuters. A Reuters poll had forecast 3%. Economic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said the economy would need to grow 6.3% in the fourth quarter to reach the lower end of the 3.5% to 4.5% full-year target. Inflation hit 7.8% in October, a more than three-year high, and the central bank has raised rates by 125 basis points since April, including a 50 basis point hike in October.
key_points: Q3 GDP growth was 2.1%, slower than the previous quarter's 2.4% and below a Reuters poll forecast of 3%.
The economy has slowed for five consecutive quarters, and growth averaged 2.5% in the first nine months.
Reaching the lower end of the 3.5% to 4.5% target needs 6.3% growth in Q4, which looks difficult.
Annual inflation reached 7.8% in October, a more than three-year high, weighing on household spending.
Infrastructure spending fell 15.1% and farm output contracted 4.8%, while the central bank has raised rates by 125 basis points since April.
stories.market_take: Weak growth alongside high inflation and rate rises could weigh on the peso and Philippine equities.

stories.headline: ‘Tents don’t protect us’: Rains flood displaced Palestinians in Gaza
stories.claim: Heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of tents in Gaza, worsening shelter crisis as aid and mobile homes remain blocked.
stories.summary: Heavy rain that began on Friday flooded displacement camps across Gaza, with Gaza's Government Media Office saying more than 70,000 tents were flooded. Displaced families in az-Zawayda and elsewhere lost mattresses, food and belongings, and some children slept standing up. Residents say the ceasefire agreement signed more than a year ago has not delivered promised mobile homes, tents and heavy machinery, which remain stuck at the Egyptian border. The UN OCHA estimates Gaza needs about 121,000 tents and 561,000 tarpaulins. Aid groups and rights monitors blame Israeli restrictions, which Israel has not accepted as a justification; the report is based on Al Jazeera's own interviews and accounts from Gaza's authorities.

stories.summary: Singapore police said four men aged between 27 and 39 will be charged in court on Tuesday, 10 November, over an alleged scheme to fraudulently obtain more than S$6 million (about US$4.68 million) in mortgage loans. The men allegedly used forged identity documents and impersonation to take loans from two credit companies, using a residential property as collateral without the owner's knowledge. Arrests were made in a two-day operation on 14 and 15 April, and police are still seeking one remaining accomplice. The charges include abetment of cheating and possessing forged identity documents.

stories.headline: Apple, Samsung turn to Chinese AI rivals to stay competitive
stories.claim: Apple and Samsung are relying on Chinese AI partners, Alibaba and Baidu, to meet rules and compete in China.
stories.summary: Apple and Samsung are increasingly depending on Chinese technology firms to provide AI services in China. Apple announced on 31 October a partnership with Alibaba to bring its Qwen model into Apple Intelligence in China, with developer testing started and a public rollout planned for December under iOS 27.3. Samsung has worked with Baidu since January 2024 to localise Galaxy AI, and its Chinese version uses Baidu's Ernie model. Experts say these tie-ups are a practical route to meeting China's regulatory requirements, although they raise concerns about dependence. Counterpoint Research says China's smartphone shipments fell 10% year on year in the third quarter, with Apple holding 19.5% share.
key_points: Apple's Qwen partnership with Alibaba was announced on 31 October, with a public rollout planned for December.
Qwen will support Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence in China.
Samsung's Galaxy AI in China relies on Baidu's Ernie model and search, and has expanded to the Galaxy S26.
Experts say the partnerships help meet regulation but raise dependence and competition risks.
Counterpoint says China's smartphone shipments fell 10% in Q3, with Huawei at 21.3% and Apple at 19.5%.
stories.market_take: Modest relevance for Apple and Samsung's China strategy; market share is expected to change little.

stories.headline: Andrej Karpathy built a curated video platform in a weekend using Claude and 20 years of Hacker News
stories.claim: Karpathy built HackerTube and TristanTube video sites in a weekend using Claude, with minimal manual work.
stories.summary: Former OpenAI co-founder and Anthropic researcher Andrej Karpathy said he built HackerTube over a weekend using Claude's Opus 5.5 model. The tool filtered 43 million Hacker News comments from 20 years of discussion to pick 6,454 recommended videos, which he said gave a better viewing experience than YouTube's recommendations. He then built TristanTube, with 47,000 videos from a channel list by Tristan Hume, which he said took about three minutes with Claude Code. Karpathy said Claude handled nearly all the work, with his only manual steps being an API key, a rented server and buying a domain. He argued that projects that once took weeks can now take a few hours. The report is based on his own posts on X.
key_points: Karpathy built HackerTube over a weekend using Claude's Opus 5.5 model.
The tool analysed 43 million Hacker News comments from 20 years to select 6,454 videos.
He says the recommendations are better than YouTube's own.
TristanTube, with 47,000 videos, was reportedly built in about three minutes with Claude Code.
His only manual steps were a Google Cloud API key, a rented server and a domain purchase.
The claims come from his own posts; no independent verification is reported.

stories.headline: I let Gemini handle my Docs, Sheets, and PDFs for a week; there's one major catch
stories.claim: Google's Gemini now lets users edit PDFs and Workspace-style files inside the chat, with limits on imported files.
stories.summary: A Android Police reviewer tested Google's Gemini over a few days for handling documents, following Google's addition of an in-chat file editor. The feature lets users open and tweak PDFs, Docs, Sheets and Slides within the conversation, highlight areas for revision and generate charts from selected content. Editing is limited to files created in Gemini or Google Workspace; arbitrary PDFs from Adobe Acrobat or scanned images are not supported. The reviewer found the desktop web version more responsive than mobile, which sometimes lagged or hung. He concluded that it will not replace Docs or Sheets yet but could become useful for casual editing.
key_points: Google has added an in-chat file editor to Gemini.
Users can edit PDFs on mobile and web, and some other formats on desktop web.
Highlighting text in a document lets Gemini revise only that selection.
Imported PDFs from outside Google's ecosystem are not supported.
The reviewer found mobile performance sluggish and the web version smoother.
The article is a personal hands-on review rather than an official announcement.

stories.headline: ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints
stories.claim: UK public bodies report being overwhelmed by AI-generated complaints, requests and legal challenges.
stories.summary: The Guardian reports that UK MPs' offices, councils, lawyers, schools and courts are receiving rising volumes of AI-generated correspondence. A Labour MP's caseworker said that half of her emails now involve some form of AI, making them harder and slower to handle. Lawyers in Local Government said complaints have grown in length, with the typical length now about ten times longer than two pages. The Information Commissioner's Office found many public authorities received more requests in 2025. Employment tribunal claims rose 28% year on year in the April to June quarter, to 14,000 single-claimant cases. Researchers have termed the trend agentic flooding, and councils say it adds cost without extra funding.
key_points: Half of emails received by one Labour MP's office are AI-generated, according to a caseworker.
Councils and legal bodies report longer, more complex complaints, some around 200 pages.
The ICO said many public authorities received more requests in 2025.
Employment tribunal claims rose 28% in April to June compared with a year earlier.
Local authorities receive no extra funding for higher volumes of complaints.
The ICO says AI-drafted requests still need human responses.
